blandish

/BLAN-dish/ - the stress falls on BLAN · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Blandish means to coax someone by flattering them.

The nephew blandished his aunt through every visit — her roses, her pastry, her violin — and drove home each time in her car.

Worked Example

Campaign staff learned to blandish the senior columnist before every interview: twenty minutes on his out-of-print books bought their nominee twenty gentle questions.

Blandish is flattery with a lever behind it. To flatter is simply to overpraise, and to wheedle is to beg sweetly and persistently — but to blandish is to warm a person with praise precisely so they will hand over the thing you want.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

butter up: To butter someone up is the playground version of blandishing — praise laid on thick right before a favor, so obvious that everyone within earshot knows it. Blandish is the courtly, bookish cousin: the same flattery-for-a-purpose, applied so smoothly the target may never notice the lever.

wheedle: To wheedle is to get your way by sweet, whiny persistence — pleading and pleading until the other person gives in just to end it. Blandish never begs: it works through praise, warming the target with compliments so that the request, when it finally comes, is hard to refuse.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

browbeat: forces agreement with threats instead of compliments

insult: slams the door that flattery tries to open

Where it sits · how self-serving the compliments are — praise → flatter → blandish

praise vs. blandish: Praise is the mildest rung and may be completely deserved — praising a speech asks for nothing back, while blandishing always does.

flatter vs. blandish: Flatter stops short of blandish: flattery merely overdoes the compliments, but blandishment aims them — the praise is a doorbell rung just before a request.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — bland-

Root — bland-: smooth, flattering (Latin blandus)

Suffix — -ish

Suffix — -ish: French verb ending, as in nourish and finish

Put it together

Put it together: Latin blandus meant smooth and flattering. French turned the root into a verb, and English kept the French verb ending -ish — the same tail you hear in nourish and finish. To blandish is to smooth a person over, stroking with words until resistance slides away. The root also survives in our adjective bland: smoothness with nothing behind it.

Use the root in a new word: bland

Use the root in a new word: bland: The hospital food was so bland that patients begged their visitors to smuggle in hot sauce.

Word Choice

formal / slightly old-fashioned

Blandish is bookish and a little courtly — the narrator's word for flattery deployed as a tool. In casual speech people say butter up or sweet-talk. Its neighbors in this unit divide the labor: beguile deceives through charm at large, and a sycophant blandishes as a way of life.
